questions.title: How can the Federal Circuit reverse a jury's infringement verdict on JMOL if it must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The jury found infringement, and the district court denied JMOL. The opinion says the Federal Circuit reviews the denial of JMOL under Fifth Circuit law and asks whether reasonable jurors could have reached the verdict, viewing the evidence favorably to the winner. But then it still reverses on both patents. What exactly makes a case cross the line from 'the jury could believe this witness' into 'no reasonable jury could find infringement'? Is the key point that the expert testimony was too internally inconsistent to count as substantial evidence at all?

questions.title: Why did the court treat the expert's contradictory mapping of claim elements as legally insufficient rather than just a credibility issue for the jury?
questions.question_body: For the '134 patent, Finesse's expert seems to have first mapped the claimed 'interference generating signals' to the 'modeled PIM path,' but that path was generated only after the RF ADC sampling step. Then, under cross, he seemed to pivot toward x1 and x2, but never clearly remapped them to the claim limitations. I thought contradictions in testimony usually go to weight and credibility, which juries decide. Why did the Federal Circuit say this kind of self-contradictory expert testimony cannot support the verdict? Is there a doctrinal rule that an expert has to provide a clear element-by-element mapping for infringement, and if the mapping is materially inconsistent the testimony stops being substantial evidence?

questions.title: In an infringement case, how precise does an expert's claim-element mapping have to be at trial?
questions.question_body: A lot of the court's reasoning seems to turn on the fact that Dr. Wells never clearly testified that x1 and x2 were the claimed 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals,' and that Finesse tried to reconstruct that mapping later by piecing together different parts of the record. Is that generally not allowed? In other words, can a patentee rely on inferences from charts, documents, and scattered testimony, or does the expert need to explicitly identify, in a coherent way, where each claim limitation is found in the accused product? I'm trying to understand whether this is a patent-specific evidentiary requirement or just a general substantial-evidence principle.

questions.title: Why wasn't changing the claim from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' considered prosecution disclaimer?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent, the accused system apparently used only two unique signals, x1 and x2, and Finesse had amended its claims during prosecution from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' after an obviousness rejection over Filipovic. My instinct was that this amendment should surrender two-signal systems. But the Federal Circuit says there was no 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal, partly because Finesse also argued Filipovic dealt with active rather than passive IMPs. How can an amendment narrowing the literal text from 'two or three' to 'three' still not give up two-signal embodiments? Is this because disclaimer is a claim-construction doctrine requiring clarity beyond what is needed for ordinary narrowing amendment purposes?

questions.title: What is the legal difference between 'three separately identifiable signals' and 'three unique signals' in this patent claim?
questions.question_body: The district court construed 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to mean 'separately identifiable' but not necessarily 'unique,' and the Federal Circuit seems to agree with that construction. I'm struggling to understand what that means in practice. If a system has only two unique input signals, how can it still satisfy a requirement for three signals? Does this mean one of the signals can be just a duplicate or another version of one of the others? And if so, what limits are there—could a signal, its conjugate, and its magnitude all count as separate signals, or does that become too far removed from the claim language?

questions.title: Why did the court say the accused radios did not perform the claimed 'seven multiplications' if some of the products might overlap mathematically?
questions.question_body: The '775 patent claims generating an nth-order ICS by digitally multiplying and filtering seven listed products involving S1, S2, and S3. The district court seemed to think that if the accused radios produced three distinct multiplications, those could correspond to the seven claimed ones because some would collapse when the inputs are not unique. But the Federal Circuit rejected that. Is the court saying the claim requires evidence that all seven listed multiplication operations are actually performed, even if some of them would evaluate to the same algebraic result? In other words, does the claim focus on the number of computational operations performed rather than the number of distinct outputs produced?

questions.title: Why couldn't Finesse rely on Nokia documents and appellate explanations to show the seven claimed multiplications were present?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Finesse tried on appeal and at oral argument to explain how Nokia's technical documents showed not just seven multiplications but ten, and how those should map to the claim. But the court says that evidence was never actually presented to the jury in a way that supported infringement. Why isn't it enough that the underlying documents were in evidence? Does patent infringement proof require the expert to walk the jury through the exact mapping at trial, rather than letting the appellate court infer it from raw exhibits? I'm trying to understand the boundary between permissible reliance on admitted technical documents and impermissible post hoc attorney reconstruction.

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the damages award instead of reaching the defendants' separate damages arguments?
questions.question_body: The defendants appealed both infringement and damages, including the denial of a new trial on damages, and the jury had awarded a large lump-sum royalty for the remaining life of the patents. But once the Federal Circuit reversed on noninfringement, it simply vacated the damages award. Is that just because damages automatically fall away when there is no liability, making the damages issues moot? And if the court had affirmed infringement on one patent but not the other, would it typically remand for a new damages trial instead of vacating the whole award?
